description: We’re Team SkyBurn, building a web app that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspot data into one clear burning-activity calendar. Our skills: software development, web development, and AI. We’re looking for teammates with Earth Science knowledge, Data Visualization skills, or a Designer to help make our dashboard look great. If you’re into satellite data, wildfires, or just want to build something impactful — join us!
summary:
Satellites have watched fires for 26 years, but the record is split across instruments whose counts cannot be compared. In Pakistan's Punjab, VIIRS detects 5.4 times more hotspots than MODIS for the same fires, because its 375 m pixels catch the small field fires that MODIS's 1 km pixels miss. Stack the two records together and 2012 shows a 600% jump that is purely the arrival of a new satellite. Anyone reading that graph would conclude burning increased sixfold.
SkyBurn puts every satellite on one scale, then builds a burning activity calendar from it. A user draws an area, and the app shows how much is burning now against the median of the same month in previous years, every month since 2000 as a colour-coded calendar, where the fires sit on a map, and when the region's fire seasons fall. Our validation shows the harmonized series lands within 1% of a known answer in every era, where the raw record is 2.5 times too high.
For Punjab the tool reports three burning seasons a year  February, May and October-November , matching the sugarcane, wheat and rice harvests. As of 14 November 2026 the region is running 35% above its November median, the second-highest November in 27 years of record.
details:
What it does

SkyBurn turns 26 years of satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar for any area a user selects. It answers four questions a fire manager actually asks: how much is burning right now compared with normal, which months and years burned most, where in the area the fires are, and when the region's fire seasons fall.

How it works

The record is split across satellites that cannot be compared directly. A MODIS hotspot is the centre of a 1 km pixel; a VIIRS hotspot is the centre of a 375 m pixel, so VIIRS detects far smaller fires. Several VIIRS satellites also flew at the same time — Suomi NPP from 2012, NOAA-20 from 2018 — so adding them together counts the same fire twice and creates a new false step at every launch.

SkyBurn treats the record as a set of platforms and places all of them on the scale of one reference platform, Suomi NPP, which overlaps MODIS at one end and NOAA-20 at the other:

  1. For each platform, measure its ratio to the reference over the period both were flying. For Punjab this gives MODIS 5.37x and NOAA-20 0.96x.
  2. Give each 0.25-degree grid cell its own ratio, shrunk toward the global ratio in proportion to how little data that cell holds.
  3. For each month use exactly one platform, never a sum — the reference where it was flying, otherwise the platform needing the least rescaling.
  4. Rescale that platform's count onto the reference.

Three statistical traps had to be handled, each found by testing against data with a known answer:

  • Selection bias. Filtering cell-months on "at least N detections in both sensors" before taking the ratio keeps only the months where the weaker sensor happened to score well. Against a known 2.6 ratio this returned 2.41. We total the whole overlap period instead.
  • Jensen's inequality. A per-cell ratio divides two noisy counts, and the expected value of such a ratio sits above the true one. Multiplying independent counts by those ratios put the MODIS era 17% above truth. Per-cell ratios now decide where activity sits; the global ratio decides how much.
  • Partial boundary months. Suomi NPP stopped on 2 November 2026, so its final month holds two days. Read as a whole month it looks like burning collapsed — and the latest month is what the current-conditions panel reports. A stopped platform's partial month is dropped and the month falls through to the next satellite.

Benefits

Fire agencies plan staff and equipment against seasonal patterns. A record with a 600% artificial step makes that planning unreliable, and nothing in the raw data announces which part of a rise is real. SkyBurn removes the step and shows, for any area, whether the current month is unusual against its own history.

The seasonal output is directly actionable. Punjab's three burning seasons line up with three harvests, which means the burning is scheduled rather than accidental, and therefore addressable by policy and timing rather than only by suppression. The same analysis runs on any region in the world.

Future potential

The harmonization method generalises to any satellite record with an overlap period, so NOAA-21 and future instruments can be added by measuring one more ratio. Natural extensions are a forecast of the coming season from the historical pattern, alerting when an area crosses its historical threshold, and overlaying meteorological data to separate weather-driven years from policy-driven ones.

Tools and technologies

Python with pandas and NumPy for the harmonization and analytics; Flask for the API; a single self-contained HTML page with Leaflet for the map and hand-written SVG for the charts; OpenStreetMap tiles. No build step and no paid services — the project runs from a clone with three commands.

The repository includes validate.py, which scores the harmonization against synthetic data with a known answer. We used it to find and fix each of the three statistical errors above.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System)
